meta.location: Shemlon, and the land of Nephi

world_behind.title: Who the priests are by now
world_behind.text: They ran when the people came to burn the king, and the record says plainly why they could not go home: they were ashamed, and they expected to be killed. They have wives and children inside a city they cannot enter. What happens in verse 5 is done by men with no community left to answer to.

world_behind.title: Twenty-four women, and what becomes of them
world_behind.text: The record does not drop them here. Three chapters on they are called the wives of these men and are sent out to plead for their husbands' lives, and the Lamanites spare the men because of them. Later still their children refuse to be called by their fathers' names. This chapter is not the last thing the record has to say about them.

world_behind.title: Collective blame, and why it looked reasonable
world_behind.text: The Lamanites assume Limhi's people are responsible, and from their side the inference is sound: Limhi's colony is the Nephite population they know is nearby. An entire people is attacked for what roughly two dozen fugitives did.

world_behind.title: How close everything is
world_behind.text: Shemlon borders Limhi's land, and Noah used to watch it from his own city. The priests are hiding in the country between, near enough to find a Lamanite gathering place and raid it, and near enough that suspicion falls at once on the closest Nephites. The whole chapter happens inside a small stretch of country.

world_behind.title: Ground instead of numbers
world_behind.text: Limhi's people lie in wait in fields and forests and attack from cover. The record says they were not half so numerous, and explains the result by motive: they fought for their lives, their wives, and their children.

world_behind.title: The argument is about a promise
world_behind.text: Verses 14 and 15 are two kings discussing which of them broke an oath. Limhi's people had sworn tribute; the Lamanite king had sworn not to slay them. Neither appeals to strength. In a chapter that opens with an abduction and a battle, the turn comes from a dispute over a word given.

words.text: Cheerful, festive, without any hint of impropriety in the older sense. Treated at 1 Nephi 18:9. It describes what the daughters had gathered to be. The only other place this record uses the phrase, a group on a ship makes themselves merry just before a storm, but nothing here casts the gathering as a fault. The verse is scene-setting, and the fault arrives in verse 5.

Dared. Treated at 1 Nephi 22:29. It is used of what the priests would not risk rather than what they could not do: they durst not return to their wives and their children. The verb places the barrier inside them, and the verse supplies both halves of it, shame and fear.

Severe, painful, hard-pressed. Treated at 1 Nephi 18:14. The battle became exceedingly sore, a formula this record reserves for the worst fighting it describes. It is the only word in the chapter that reports what the fighting was like from the inside.

A military commander, and it is the office Gideon now holds under the new king. The man introduced two chapters ago as a private enemy of the crown is now the crown's officer, and his first recorded act in the post is to stop the king from executing his own people.

To calm an anger already in motion, as distinct from preventing one. Every use of it here is transitive and takes a person as its object: pacify them, pacify the king, pacified towards us. Nobody in the chapter is asked to be reasonable; somebody is asked to do the calming.

Weapons. The Lamanite king proposes that both sides go out to meet the armies carrying none, and the record repeats the condition three times in three verses, as if to make certain it is not read as a figure of speech.

phrases.text: Five words for a decision that took time. The priests had tarried in the wilderness, discovered the gathering place, and then waited for a day when only a few came. The record gives the premeditation its own clause and does not soften it.

phrases.term: They thought it was the people of Limhi
phrases.text: The mistake the chapter turns on, stated as a thought. The Lamanites are not accused of bad faith. They drew the available conclusion, and everything that follows (the army, the battle, the wounded king) comes from an inference nobody was in a position to correct.

phrases.term: Limhi had discovered them from the tower
phrases.text: The son using his father's monument as an instrument. What Noah built to look out over land he did not own is now a lookout in a real emergency, and the warning it gives is what lets an outnumbered people choose their ground.

phrases.term: They fought like lions for their prey
phrases.text: An image that puts the defenders in the predator's place, and the phrase occurs once in scripture. The next verse adds dragons. These are the only two similes in the chapter, and both are spent on people fighting for their families rather than on an army.

phrases.term: Ye shall not slay him, but bring him hither that I may see him
phrases.text: A king refusing his own people the killing they have just asked for. The soldiers had said let us slay him; Limhi answers with an order and then a question about an oath. The refusal comes before he knows anything about why the war started.

phrases.term: I pray thee forbear, and do not search this people
phrases.text: Gideon stopping an investigation that would have produced an execution. He had spared a king he could have killed; here he spares a population his king was about to search. Both times he moves against the momentum in the room.

phrases.term: Are not the words of Abinadi fulfilled, which he prophesied against us
phrases.text: The theological summary of the whole unit, spoken by a soldier in the middle of a military emergency. No prophet is present. The captain supplies the interpretation himself, names the man who gave it, and attributes the cause to not hearkening.

phrases.term: It is better that we should be in bondage than that we should lose our lives
phrases.text: A calculation stated flatly and never argued with. The sentence accepts tribute, guards, and a foreign king as the price of survival, and the chapter ends with the arrangement intact. It occurs once in scripture.

verses.label: v. 6–8
verses.title: A war begun on a correct inference from wrong evidence
verses.text: The Lamanites conclude that the people of Limhi took their daughters, and the record states the reasoning without correcting it yet: "they were angry with the people of Limhi, for they thought it was the people of Limhi." The whole campaign proceeds on that basis for fifteen verses. Verse 8 has Limhi discovering the army "from the tower," the same structure king Noah climbed at Mosiah 19:5, and this time it is used for reconnaissance rather than escape.

verses.label: v. 10–11
verses.title: One comparison, and one number
verses.text: The battle gets a single figure of speech, "they fought like lions for their prey," which occurs once in the volume. It gets one quantity as well, and the quantity is a ratio rather than a count: the people of Limhi "were not half so numerous as the Lamanites." No dead are counted on either side in this chapter. A battle that decides the fate of a nation is reported with a simile and a fraction.

verses.label: v. 15–16
verses.title: Two men who each know half of it
verses.text: The record has the Lamanite king state a grievance that is accurate as far as it goes: "I have broken the oath because thy people did carry away the daughters of my people; therefore, in my anger I did cause my people to come up to war." Limhi's reply reports his own ignorance: "Limhi had heard nothing concerning this matter; therefore he said: I will search among my people and whosoever has done this thing shall perish." Both men are telling the truth, and neither has the piece the other needs.

verses.label: v. 24–26
verses.title: An army disarmed as an argument
verses.text: The Lamanite king proposes a demonstration rather than a message: "Let us go forth to meet my people, without arms before them." The phrase without arms stands in three verses of the volume and all three are here, in verses 24, 25 and 26. It is used first as the king's proposal, then as the report of what they did, then as the thing the Lamanites saw. The chapter that opened with men hiding in a wood ends with men walking into an army carrying nothing.

chapter.title: The tower appears a third time, and this is its best use
chapter.text: Built so a king could look down on his neighbors, used once as an escape from a swordsman, and used here to see an army in time. Noah's vanity project is what gives his son a chance to survive.

chapter.title: Gideon prevents a second killing
chapter.text: He put up his sword at Noah's plea in chapter 19 and stops a search that would have executed innocent people here. Both interventions run against the momentum of everyone else in the room, and both times he is right.

chapter.title: A soldier delivers the theological verdict
chapter.text: Verse 21 gives the summary of everything since chapter 11: Abinadi's words fulfilled because they would not hearken. The speaker is the king's captain in the middle of a crisis. This record does not reserve interpretation for prophets.

chapter.title: The chapter's real subject is stated in one repeated verb
chapter.text: Pacify appears five times in eight verses, which is more than in any other chapter of this record. Nobody in the second half is trying to win; every speaker is trying to calm somebody down.

chapter.title: Two kings each decline the obvious move
chapter.text: Limhi refuses to let his people kill a wounded enemy king. That king then bows himself down and pleads for Limhi's people. The chapter resolves because the two men with the most reason to strike do not.

chapter.title: Going unarmed works, and the chapter says why
chapter.text: Verse 24 has the king propose it as a tactic, "Let us go forth to meet my people, without arms," and verse 26 reports the effect, "when the Lamanites saw the people of Limhi, that they were without arms, they had compassion on them and were pacified." Alma 24:21–22 has a different people do the same thing as a covenant and reports a comparable result on the same nation, that the attackers "began to be pierced for the murders which they had committed" and a thousand and five were spared. One is a stratagem and one is an oath, and the record gives both the same outcome.

chapter.title: The record puts the blame in exactly one place
chapter.text: The daughters are described as gathered to sing and dance and nothing more. Verse 18 names the priests. No speaker in the chapter, including the Lamanite king, suggests any other account.

chapter.title: Role in the unit
chapter.text: Chapter 19 leaves Limhi a kingdom on a lease; this is its first crisis; 21 brings the failed rebellions and deeper bondage; 22 brings the escape. The arrangement survives here on the strength of two men who would not kill and one captain who would not let a search proceed.

applications.title: Test the inference before you judge the motive
applications.text: The Lamanites concluded the obvious thing from the evidence they had. When someone blames you wrongly, it is worth asking what their information looked like before deciding they acted in bad faith.

applications.title: Do not investigate before you have listened
applications.text: Limhi's first instinct was a search with an execution attached. One person in the room knew something he did not. Ask who might already have the answer before setting a process in motion.

applications.title: Refuse the killing while still ignorant
applications.text: Limhi stopped his people from executing a prisoner while he still had no idea why the war had started. Restraint is worth more when it is exercised early and without justification in hand.

applications.title: Look for the use in what was built badly
applications.text: A monument to vanity turned out to be a watchtower. Something in your situation that was made for the wrong reasons may still be the only instrument you have.

applications.title: Say what the cost of survival actually is
applications.text: Better bondage than death is not a noble sentence, and nobody in the chapter pretends otherwise. When a hard choice is the right one, naming it plainly beats dressing it up.

applications.title: Empty hands can do what arguments cannot
applications.text: Two speeches had not settled anything; the sight of an unarmed crowd did. Consider what could be visibly given up in a standoff, and what that would communicate that words have not.

applications.title: Put the blame where it belongs and leave it there
applications.text: The chapter never drifts toward the victims. When you are accounting for something that went wrong, notice any pull toward spreading responsibility onto people who were only present.

questions.text: What am I not going back to when shame is the only thing stopping me?
Whom have I judged on an inference I never went back to check?
When have I stopped something bad from happening before I understood the situation?
Who has told me to forbear, and did I listen?
What in my life is a consequence I already know the cause of?
What would it take for me to be the one who bows first?
